newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rio +5 study strongly critical of gov't subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Rio +5 study strongly critical of gov't subsidies.

text.p: Governments spend an estimated $700 billion to $900 billion a year on subsidies that do more harm than good to the economy and the environment, a study released on Wednesday said.

The study by the Dutch Institute for Research on Public Expenditure, released at the end of the Rio +5 environment conference, concluded that many subsidies in agriculture, water, energy and road transportation no longer serve their original purposes. It said they harm the environment and serve the rich rather than the poor.

"Governments North and South are using hard-earned tax revenues to subsidise unsustainable development," said James MacNeill, chairman of the steering committee for the report. "They are undermining the Earth with public funds."
Major developed countries were responsible for roughly two-thirds of these subsidies, comparable to worldwide arms spending, said Andre de Moor, the author of the report.

The study showed that $335 billion in annual agriculture subsidies encourage unsustainable production including the overuse of pesticides and fertilisers. Subsidisation of irrigation water is a major cause of soil salinization, which reduces food production.

In the energy sector, industrialised countries spend between $70 billion and $80 billion on subsidies that encourage excessive use of fossil fuels, which contribute to pollution, acid rain and global warming, the report said. Road transportation is subsidised with $100 billion to $215 billion a year in industrialised and developing countries, contributing to air pollution, urban sprawl and traffic congestion.
The report also concluded that politicians and industry are "addicted" to these subsidies and that reform faces strong opposition from vested interests.
"The primary benefit of subsidies is political," MacNeill said. "I have yet to meet many politicians who are willing to give up this proven path to power."
He said it was necessary to show politicians ways they could achieve the political benefits while at the same time helping the economy, the environment and the poor.
De Moor said subsidies had to be reformed and eliminated to remove their negative effects on the environment.

Hundreds of environmentalists, business leaders and United Nations officials met at the weeklong Rio +5 conference, which closed on Wednesday, to review and revive the pledges made by heads of state at the Earth Summit in 1992.
